characters: Esaaba: an eleven-year-old Ghanaian girl with braided hair tied back with a blue ribbon, wearing a neat blue-and-amber school uniform and carrying a lined exercise book and pencil.
Nana Ama Serwaa: a dignified elderly Ghanaian woman with silver hair, wearing a warm amber-and-indigo traditional cloth wrapper, seated on a carved low wooden stool in a shady courtyard.
Class teacher: a smiling Ghanaian teacher in a crisp collared shirt holding the bound class storybook.

narrationPlan.voice: A polite, bright girl’s voice for Esaaba; a warm, unhurried elder’s voice for Nana Ama Serwaa
narrationPlan.pace: Warm, attentive, and steady (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A soft, slow drum and gentle humming (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Oral traditions belong to the storytellers and communities who carry them. Asking permission, listening without interrupting, checking accuracy, and crediting the teller by name are core ethical practices in oral history.
If an elder prefers that a particular family or sacred account not be written down, learners must respect that refusal cheerfully.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm that the five fieldwork steps align with local community expectations and school project guidelines.

teacherGuide.overview: A practical, respectful model of oral-history fieldwork for upper primary and JHS learners: permission, active listening, checking back, and attribution.
learningGoals: List the steps for collecting an oral story ethically.
Explain why we read a draft back and credit the storyteller.
Practise polite interview questions with a partner.
beforeReading: Ask: if you tell a friend your own story and they share it as theirs, how do you feel?
whileReading: Pause on page 4: why did Esaaba read her draft back to Nana Ama Serwaa?
afterReading: With family permission, collect a short proverb or folktale at home and credit the teller, date, and town.
Compile a class anthology celebrating local storytellers.
discussion: Why do date, place, and storyteller’s name matter when preserving oral history?
reflection: Which elder in your family or neighbourhood would you love to listen to?

support: Give learners a simple interview template: Teller’s Name, Place, Date, Story, Checked With Teller.
stretch: Collect two tellings of a well-known tale from two elders and note how each teller makes it unique.

culturalNotes: Oral traditions belong to the storytellers and communities who carry them. Asking permission, listening without interrupting, checking accuracy, and crediting the teller by name are core ethical practices in oral history.
If an elder prefers that a particular family or sacred account not be written down, learners must respect that refusal cheerfully.
localiseThis: Keep original home-language terms alongside clear English explanations, just as Esaaba kept Nana’s Twi words.

reviewerNotes: Confirm Akan/Ghanaian tone and vowel length.
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.
